en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wenyi of Qingliang Monastery in Jinling,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Yufeng of Mount Jing, Yuanxin, Wudi Dizhu, and Guo Ningzhi.
The Master’s courtesy name was Wenyi;
he was the son of the Ru family of Yuhang.
At the age of seven,
he shaved his head under Chan Master Quanwei of Xinding Zhitong Monastery.
He was still young.
He received his full ordination at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou under the Vinaya master Master Xijue.
He flourished in his propagation of the teachings at Yuyang Temple on Mount Baohua in Mingzhou.
The Master went there beforehand to listen to and study [the teachings],
thoroughly investigating their subtle principles;
he further explored the Confucian classics in parallel.
Master Jue frequented the circles of literary elegance;
his contemporaries regarded him as our school’s own Yan Hui and Zixia.
Once the Master had unleashed his profound spiritual mechanism,
all miscellaneous affairs were cast aside;
he then struck his mendicant’s staff and journeyed southward.
He arrived at Fuzhou to visit Changqing,
but did not achieve great enlightenment.
Later, he wished to leave the mountain ranges along with three others, including Shaofa and Jin.
Passing through Jizai-in,
we were hindered by snow;
resting for a short while, we sat beside the brazier.
Jizang asked,
"Where are you going on this journey?
The Master replied:
"I am going on a pilgrimage," [the monk] said. Dizang asked,
"What is the matter of pilgrimage?"
The Master said,
"I do not know.
Dizang said:
He did not know that this was most intimate.
Furthermore, the three of them together cited the *Zhao lun*;
when they reached the passage, "Heaven and earth share the same root as I," [he suddenly realized].
Dizang said, "The mountains,
rivers, and the great earth,
as well as your own self, O Venerable One."
"Are they the same or different?
The Master said,
"Different."
Dizang held up two fingers.
The Master said, "The same."
Jizang then held up two fingers and immediately departed.
Xueji took his leave and went away.
Dizang sent him off at the gate and asked, "Upādhyāya,
you usually say that the three realms are mind-only."
"All phenomena are but consciousness.
Pointing to a stone in the courtyard, he said, "Now tell me: [what is it?]"
"Is this stone within the mind or outside the mind?
The Master said,
"It is within the mind."
Dizang said,
"A wandering monk—
what need has he for such pretexts? Why place a mere fragment of stone upon his heart?"
The Master was at a loss for a reply;
he immediately set down his bundle, sat beneath the mat,
and sought a definitive resolution.
For nearly a month,
he presented his views and explained the principles.
Kṣitigarbha spoke to him, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is not like that," [the Master] said.
The teacher replied, "I am at my wits' end; my reasoning has reached its limit."
Dizang said,
"If one speaks of the Buddha-dharma,
everything is already fully realized."
The Master attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. Consequently,
they discussed whether he should remain,
and the Master and his companions advanced [to accept the invitation].
Desiring to tour the monastic centers throughout the region south of the Yangtze River,
he ordered the Master to accompany him;
they arrived at Linchuan.
The Provincial Governor requested that he reside at Chongshu Temple.
He opened the hall for formal discourse;
by midday, he was seated at the tea ceremony and had not yet risen.
At that time, the Sangha Rectifier addressed the Master, saying,
"The fourfold assembly has already gathered around;
the Dharma seat of the Upādhyāya is prepared."
The Master said,
"Everyone should instead study with a true spiritual friend.
After a short while, he ascended the hall.

"The great assembly has gathered like clouds;
we pray that the Master will proclaim the Dharma."
The Master said,
"The assembly has been standing for a long time," and then he spoke.
Since everyone is gathered here,
this mountain monk cannot remain silent;
I shall cite a skillful means of an ancient master for the sake of the great assembly.
"Take care. He then descended from his seat.

At these words, the disciple suddenly attained a clear realization and composed a verse to express his sincere devotion.

the Master, through subtle means, stimulated them to awaken,
and they all gradually came to internalize his teachings.

[He] ascends the hall.

Furthermore, does the principle of the Buddha-dharma exist or not?
Try to explain it.

"And why have you come here? If there were [any],

In which teaching does such a moment exist? If it exists, [then speak].
Try to bring it up and see.
Is it not that there are such words within the scriptures?
Is this the right time?

Therefore it is said:

ultimate reality dwells before one's eyes, yet it is instead perceived as a realm of manifold phenomena.
Furthermore, how can one turn it over?

how can one make it right?
Do you understand?

Do not say that asking such a question is itself unacceptable;
you should say that the six sense bases are without sound,

The ear-faculty does not know sound.
If it were fundamentally existent,
how could one understand its non-existence?
The ancients said:
"To be free from sound and form, yet become attached to sound and form;
to be free from names and words, yet become attached to names and words."
Therefore, although one attains it through cultivation in the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva-deva),
after eighty thousand great kalpas have passed,
one may suddenly fall away from it in a single day.
All matters appear solemn and formal;
this is because one does not know the fundamental reality and thus practices according to a gradual sequence.
In three births, sixty kalpas are completed;
in four births, one hundred kalpas.
In this manner, one proceeds until the fruit is perfected after three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.

"It is not as good as realizing in a single thought that dependent origination is unborn,
thereby transcending the provisional views of those who study the three vehicles."
Furthermore, it is said:
"A single snap of the fingers perfectly accomplishes the eighty thousand gates;
in a single kṣaṇa, the three great kalpas are extinguished."
One must also investigate this through direct experience.
